name: Fula (Fulani, Peul)
subtitle: Fula (Fulani, Peul): who the sources name, where they live, and what the old labels got wrong.

keyPoints.text: About 30,000,000 people (2025): Courtright's estimate for the Fulani community as a whole (not a count of speakers), 'spread across at least 19 African countries'.
Fula, Fulani, Fulbe and Peul are names for the same community: 'Fulbe' is used in their own languages and 'Peul' in French.
The language is called Pulaar or Fulfulde (Peul in French); INALCO gives the double name.

parts.text: The language is called Pulaar or Fulfulde (Peul in French); INALCO gives the double name.

Speakers: INALCO estimates over 20 million (undated, no method given); the language is spoken in about twenty West and Central African states. Estimates differ between sources and no single census counts speakers.

A language survey lists 17 African countries with Fulfulde speakers (Burkina Faso, Benin, CAR, Cote d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Ghana, Gambia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Nigeria, Sudan, Senegal, Chad, Togo).
The community is internally varied: many languages and cultural systems, and a settled majority.
Many Fulani settled long ago: in the Guinea highlands they settled permanently in large urban centres centuries ago and developed complex agricultural systems.
Fulani live as a minority in every country where they are found, across at least 19 states.
Colonial administrative logic did not fit local realities; independent states inherited borders that left Fulani dispersed as minorities in several countries (press article; tier uncertain).
In Niger 1890-1920, borders led colonial administrators to monitor livestock movements more closely, though state control over mobile herders was limited.

blocks.q: Myth or fact: All Fulani are nomadic herders who migrate with cattle.
blocks.explain: The source says transhumance is often imagined for all Fulani but in reality the vast majority are settled.

items.text: The jihad led by Uthman dan Fodio against the Hausa dynasty of Gobir (declared February 1804) led to the Sokoto Caliphate, run largely as a federation of emirates.

A series of Fulani-led religious revolutions produced Islamic states across West Africa. The Macina state (1818-1853) is only named as the title of a cited book (Ba & Daget); no readable page on Macina was found.

Under colonial rule power shifted to new capitals and a Western-educated elite; settled Fulani leaders were incorporated into colonial and post-colonial governments, but rural, semi-nomadic communities were not.

After independence, droughts in the 1970s-80s hit Sahelian herds, and in the early 2010s a pastoralism crisis reached a critical point in the central Sahel and Nigeria; the author attributes violence to several unconnected groups and says the whole community has been blamed (author's analysis).
